title: How to start writing about film aged 15?

commenti.body:
Start by keeping a journal and writing notes about every film you watch. Be that guy who brings a journal to movie nights w your friends. 

When you find something good you haven't read online, write it up and post it in r/flicks or r/truefilm. See how people respond.

This is a marathon, not a race. You will need to grind at this for years. Which shouldnt be a problem, you love it.

The best advice I heard lately is pick a niche. If you want to transition to writing a blog, YouTuber, etc, you have to have a niche. Then you develop a targeted audience you cater to that keep coming back because you're the only voice speaking to them. A niche would be like music in 1970s horror, true film that focuses on animals, south east asias take on folk horror. You need genre and then some way to look at that genre in a new way.

I would start with movies you love.

And a skill I think every writer should work on who is trained through basic school is making your writing tighter and more focus.

Write on scenes and not whole movies or genres.

And the best method I got also was 3 drafts. Let's say final project needs to be 12 pages 

1st draft) outline-well detailed.  
2nd draft 15 pages essay
Final draft) 12 pages and mostly you editing stuff out.

Also while in school use the other subjects in school. It is easy. You are already reading other books and subjects. Apply those lense to your movie watching and writing. And vice versa.


Oh also find people you trust to edit and write stuff also. We are so ial beings and being a social writer helps.

I’d try to get into Columbia. Film studies major, English minor. Going cheap is always a risk. The horror stories about UNCSA and Guilford are the stuff of legend. Right now, really take your high school English classes seriously. 

My parents never kept films from me. I was an extremely lucky child. I got to see Silence of the Lambs at 9 years old. It’s integral to cultivate a deep interest in film. In horror id suggest Psycho and Baby Jane. Citizen Kane and Rashomon are required. Every teen should be able to binge John Waters. I recently rewatched Whore, and it’s so much better than I originally thought as a kid. Every teen deserves the opportunity to watch Lady Snowblood, Foxy Brown, and Coffy. And Striptease. Flashdance. The Turning Point. Every teen deserves the right to watch Ice Castles and to decide on the mood they feel. Gorillas in the Mist. Elle, La Pianiste! I ❤️ Huckabees. It’s integral to challenge yourself. Pulp Fiction and Jackie Brown. Parasite. Feel confidence and amazement as you dive in to this glorious art form.

you can start building experience in high school, if there's a school newspaper or a film club then get active in those organizations and make your desires and skills known. if a club doesn't exist see if you can form a new one. i did something similar in high school when I wanted to write music criticism.

use an app like letterboxd or imdb to keep track of the films you watch and your opinions on them 

watch movies about subject matter you don't think you care about so you can expand your horizons.

read a lot of criticism. Pauline Kael's work is studied in college courses on film criticism, check her out. AO Scott is another one. I also found myself reading a lot of Chuck Klosterman when I was a little older than you, but he does cultural criticism beyond film as well like his focus on music.

try watching a lot of films by a single director so you can see what stays consistent from film to film, understand an individual artist's style.

when you watch old films, try to figure out the context around them when they were released. movies make more sense when you know the culture that produced them.

You're 15, so I'd recommend you learn while you do. What I mean by that is prioritize learning the crafts of both film and writing (specifically writing critique), but also don't wait to start practicing and doing. So many people do reviews for the films they watch (as a hobby) - some even are near-annoying about it, posting self-promoting posts on this sub, always with links to their cache of reviews, written and/or as video. Do the same thing. Personally, I'd rather see a 15 year old do that than someone in their 20s or 30s.

Personally, I'd consider aiming your voice at your own age group. Helping other kids understand what they might be overlooking as casual viewers could be very important and needed. Most people (which includes kids) won't read long reviews, but that doesn't mean you shouldn't practice writing them. They can always be available at a host sight. Your practice could also include shorter reviews. Websites, newspapers, magazines - they all have word count limits for review submissions, so you need to learn that part of the craft. And then, don't be shy about doing a video version. It's all a lot of work - none of this is an easy or short journey - but all the discovery and achievement in the journey will keep you enchanted and passionate for at least the next decade.

Best of luck.

Film critic here. 

The thing about film criticism is that social media has made everyone into a critic. So you really need to find a niche and style that you can own. The days of simply saying a movie is good or bad are gone. And writing standard reviews the way you see people do on Roger Ebert’s site just…don’t matter anymore.  

People turn to critics these days for curation, entertainment, and/or insight. If you can do one of those three things (or all of them) very well, then you’ll find a place.

For me, my expertise is in the literary side of things. So I explain themes and endings and the like. And do so in long form articles.

At 15, the thing to do is just watch a lot of movies and study up on the craft of movie making and storytelling. Find the genres you like to watch. And find the mediums of expression you enjoy. Personally, I can write 10,000 words but I have no interest in doing formal video editing the way some of those YouTube explainers do. Just like they have no interest in written content. 

You see people who are successful because they love horror movies and made a podcast to talk about horror movies. Others who hate podcasting but love TikTok so are popular on there.

The other big advice: remember you are not superior to the movies you’re reviewing. A lot of critics have main character syndrome and talk about cinema as if they’re the high arbiter of what’s good or not. It’s disrespectful to the entire industry and all the people who spent long, hard hours making a movie. You don’t have to love everything or praise everything. Just be aware that you’re a single voice and not the end all be all of judgment. It’s your opinion. Not an objective ruling.
Thank you! I can always trust r/truefilm to give really detailed, helpful answers.
